It has been a challenge to employ machine learning (ML) to optimize casting processes due to the
scarcity of data and difﬁculty in feature expansion. Here, we introduce a nearest neighbor search
method to optimize the stratiﬁed random sampling in Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) and propose a
new revised LHS coupled with Bayesian optimization (RLHS-BO). Using this method, we optimized
the squeeze-casting process for mine fuel tank partition castings for the ﬁrst time with an ultra-small
dataset of 25 samples. Compared to traditional methods such as random sampling, interval sampling,
orthogonal design (OD), and central composite design (CCD), our approach covers the process
parameter space more, reduces the data volume by approximately 50%, and achieves process
optimization beyond ﬁve factors-ﬁve levels with fewer data. Through RLHS and 6 iterations of
experiments, the optimal process was identiﬁed, and the ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of partition
casting under the optimal process reached 239.7 MPa, with an elongation (EL) of 12.2%, showing
increases of 17.6% and 18.4% over the optimal values in the initial dataset. Finally, a combination of
Shapley additive interpretation (SHAP) and phase-ﬁeld method (PFM) of solidiﬁcation dendrite growth
was used to address the issue of weak physical interpretability in ML models.
Mines, integral to underwater defense systems, signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the
designandefﬁcacyofmodernnavalstrategies.Theireffectivenesshingesnot
only on detection and strike capabilities but also on the robustness and
durability of the structure. A key component of mine is the fuel compart-
ment partition. It safeguards fuel storage while withstanding high-pressure
underwater conditions and potential mechanical impacts. Consequently,
the partition must exhibit superior UTS and EL. High UTS maintains
structural integrity under external pressure, while good EL enables plastic
deformation, absorbing, and dispersing impact forces to mitigate the risk of
brittle fracture. Squeeze-casting technology, prized for its capacity to yield
castings with dense structure, superior mechanical properties, and precise
molding, is now a preferred method for crafting partitions. Once the
material and casting gating system are established, optimization of casting
processes, such as pouring temperature, die temperature, squeeze pressure,
and dwell time, are crucial for achieving castings of exceptional quality1.
The problem that exists with traditional empirical trial-and-error
methods, which is limited by time, material, and labor costs, becomes even
more apparent in the optimization of casting processes. Design of experi-
ment (DoE), such as full factor design2, OD3, and response surface method4,
has been employed to enhance the efﬁciency of process optimization.
However, when confronted with multiple factors (process parameters) and
levels (process range), the cost required for DoE signiﬁcantly escalates.
Additionally, casting numerical simulation techniques, especially some
casting software such as ProCAST5, Magmasoft6, Flow3D7, EasyCast8, etc.,
can offer valuable process optimization insights prior to production.
Nevertheless, numerical simulation depends on precise material thermo-
physical parameters and necessitates expert analysis of the results. More-
over, most simulation results are qualitative. Establishing a quantitative
relationship between the casting process and properties through numerical
simulation is challenging9–11. Consequently, there is an urgent demand for a
more efﬁcient strategy that directly optimizes casting performance.
Developments in ML provide fresh insights into process optimization.
Data-driven ML utilizes predictive models to capture intricate relationships
between inputs and outputs, and its applications encompass material

classiﬁcation12, properties prediction13, material design14, and beyond.
Typically, casting properties15–17 or related indicators (e.g., secondary den-
drite arm spacing18, defect occurrence probability19,20, quality metrics21, etc.)
function as outputs (target values) in ML models, with process parameters
and other inﬂuencing factors (equipment, environment, etc.) as input fea-
tures. These ML models can either reveal the distribution of target values or
be integrated with optimization algorithms such as genetic algorithms and
particle swarm optimization22–25 to attain process optimization.
The effectiveness of using ML for process optimization hinges on high-
precision models, which, in turn, depend on the quality and quantity of
datasets. While actual production yields high-quality data, amassing sub-
stantial data suitable for ML within a short timeframe is impractical.
Accurate ML prediction models usually require hundreds, thousands, or
even tens of thousands of data points15–19,24,26,27. Sun et al.28 reported that a
speciﬁc part produced in a foundry annually ranges only from 300 to 7000
units, and pointed out the small size of the casting dataset. Small datasets
frequently result in imbalanced data, overﬁtting, or underﬁtting of models29.
Numerical simulation is an optional method for constructing and
expanding ML datasets in the casting process23,30–32. However, it is crucial to
consider the errors and computational costs associated with numerical
simulation, as well as the persistence of quantitative relationship issues
mentioned above. Therefore, efﬁciently optimizing processes entails
addressing the key challenge of performing ML on a relatively limited
experimental dataset.
To achieve high accuracy with small datasets, traditional ML requires
appropriate input features (descriptors)14,33. Identifying optimal descriptors
for speciﬁc tasks involves feature extension based on domain knowledge,
commonlyusedinmaterialdesign34–37.Forexample,descriptorslikeaverage
valence electron concentration, average density, average bulk modulus, and
average Poisson’s ratio are calculated based on material composition and
physical properties. However, this method is not applicable to casting
process parameters such as temperature and pressure, which lack inherent
physical and chemical properties. Thus, the customization of ML strategies
for casting processes is imperative. In addition, interpretability in ML can
enhance understanding of decision-making and optimization. Common
methodsincludefeatureimportancerankingsfromtreemodels38,regression
model weight coefﬁcients39, SHAP40, and local interpretable model-agnostic
explanations (LIME)41. These approaches focus on feature contributions
and clarify the positive and negative relationships between inputs and
outputs. However, they still require expert knowledge and physical features
for accurate application, and the underlying physical phenomena remain
unclear. Achieving intuitive physical interpretability remains a challenge in
applying ML to materials science.
In this study, we introduced a method to optimize partition parts
squeeze-casting processes with a tiny dataset by RLHS-BO. Furthermore,
the synergistic application of SHAP and PFM enhanced physical inter-
pretability. Our strategy is easilyextended to other casting methods, offering
collaborative optimization across a broader range of parameters at
lower costs.
Methods
We employed the ﬂow outlined in Fig. 1 to optimize the squeeze-casting
process for an aluminum alloy partition part efﬁciently. Fig. 1 comprises
three main stages:
1. Initial dataset size determination: Input all available squeeze process
parameters into the gðxÞ function to construct an analog dataset, with
process parameters as input and gðxÞ results as output. Create datasets
ofvaryingsizesthroughsamplingandestablishMLmodels.Determine
the optimal dataset size by balancing model accuracy and dataset size,
and use this size as the initial dataset for subsequent squeeze process
optimization.
2. Data collection: RLHS was utilized to select representative samples
(process parameters) to generate the initial dataset according to the
optimal dataset size. Squeeze-casting experiments were conducted to
obtain UTS and EL of castings.
3. Bayesian optimization:Multiple ML models were employed to develop
predictive models based on the initial dataset. The best model was
selected as the surrogate model through comparison. Potentially
optimal process parameters in unlabeled datasets (excluding experi-
mental points from step 2) were identiﬁed through expected
improvement query strategies, followed by experimental validation.
The resulting experimental data was incorporated into the initial
dataset to update the surrogate model.
The production enterprise of partition parts, Shanxi Pingyang Heavy
Industry Machinery Co., Ltd. requires partition parts to have a
UTS ≥225 MPa and an EL ≥10.5%, with a development cycle of 10months
based on production experience. Consequently, stage 3 would be reiterated
until either casting properties attained the set target or no substantial
enhancement in properties is observed.

We sequentially selected 15, 18, 20, 23, 25, 28, 30, 33, 35,50, 500,
and 2000 data points from analogous datasets using random sampling,
interval sampling, and RLHS, respectively. LHS is a stratiﬁed random
procedure that provides an efﬁcient way of sampling variables from
their multivariate distributions, which ensures uniform distribution
along each dimension46. An example of LHS is shown in Fig. S1 of
Supplementary Information. Since LHS randomly samples within a
layered range of each parameter, the obtained points may not belong to
valid process combinations in a given discrete integer process design
space, making it unsuitable for step-partitioned datasets. Therefore,
the nearest neighbor search method k-dimensional tree (cKDtree)47
was introduced to identify the process parameter design value closest to
the LHS point. cKDtree provides faster query speeds for high-
dimensional datasets than methods like linear search, vantage point
tree, rectangle tree, and ball tree, and is simpler to implement and more
accurate than approximation algorithms such as locality-sensitive
hashing, hierarchical navigable small world, and approximate nearest
neighbors oh yeah48,49. LHS revised by cKDtree ensures a uniform
distribution of samples and guarantees that all sampling points are
valid process combinations in the design space, as shown in Fig. S1 of
the Supplementary Information.
Xu et al.29 mentioned support vector machines (SVM), Gaussian
process regression (GPR), random forests (RF), gradient-boosted deci-
sion trees (GBDT), and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) as algo-
rithms suitable for modeling small datasets. In order to obtain
appropriate and accurate prediction models, we further incorporated the
least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) and Bayesian
ridge regression (BR) as comparative models. 25% of the dataset was used
as the test set. Considering the varying orders of magnitude among
process parameters, the dataset was standardized (formula in Eq. S1 of
Supplementary Information). The hyper-parameters of each model were
optimized through cross-validation and grid search. The optimal dataset
size was determined by balancing the performance of each ML model on
the remaining unselected data and the size of the dataset used. This
optimal size was then used as the initial dataset for subsequent squeeze-
casting process optimization. The coefﬁcient of determination R2 served
as evaluation indicators as shown in Eq. S2 of Supplementary
Information.
Data collection
RLHS was usedto sample the process design space (5400 process sets) based
on the optimal initial dataset size determined in the section “Initial dataset
size determination”. Subsequently, squeeze-casting experiments were con-
ducted based on these samples to establish an initial dataset comprising
squeeze-casting process parameters, UTS, and EL. Details of the squeeze-
casting process are provided in Supplementary Information. Figure 2
illustrates the distribution of process parameter sample points across the
design space, demonstrating the uniform distribution achieved through
RLHS. Figure 2d reveals a conﬂict between UTS and EL within the
highlighted red area, indicating the need for synergistic enhancement
through process optimization.
Bayesian optimization
Following the ML ﬂow from the section “Initial dataset size determination”,
ML models were established to predict UTS and EL using initial squeeze-
castingdataset.These modelswere comparedtoselectthe optimalsurrogate
model. Meanwhile, mean absolute error (MAE) was introduced as an
additional evaluation indicator (formula in Eq. S3 of Supplementary
Information).
The surrogate model had the theoretical capability to predict UTS and
EL of partition parts manufactured through different squeeze-casting pro-
cesses. However, despite utilizing RLHS to achieve the best possible cov-
erage, the training data still has limited representation compared to the
expansive design space of process parameters. Consequently, notable
uncertainties persisted when applying the model to the entire design
domain50. To enhance process optimization efﬁciency, BO51 accounting for
uncertainty was employed in this study. The expected improvement (EI)
was selected as the acquisition function due to its efﬁcient global optimi-
zation (EGO)50, as shown in Eq. (2):

Interpretability
In this study, we enhanced the physical interpretability of data-driven
optimization by integrating SHAP with the PFM. Initially, SHAP is
employed to identify critical processes affecting casting properties, a task
traditionally demanding substantial experimental and analytical efforts in
numerical simulations. Subsequently, these key process factors were lever-
aged as variables within the PFM to further enrich the physical under-
standing of optimization outcomes. PFM has shown great potential in
material design and mechanism interpretation52–58. A quantitative phase-
ﬁeld model was used to describe α-Al dendrite growth of ZL101 alloy under
pressure in this study, supplementing the potential optimization principles
of our strategy. The PFM of this study is based on the solidiﬁcation module
in EasyPhase software, which is a comprehensive phase-ﬁeld theory soft-
ware package developed bythe group of Prof. Yuhong Zhao59,60. The speciﬁc
PFM model is detailed in the Supplementary Information.

Results
Selection results of initial dataset size
Figure 3 displays R2 values for ML models constructed from diverse analog
dataset sizes using different sampling methods. Notably, models based on
RLHS outperformed random and interval sampling in terms of R2 values.
Accuracy across all ML models improved with increasing training data. The
performance of ML models varied signiﬁcantly within the small dataset of
this study, attributed to the limited data leading to reduced information
learned by the ML model and poor generalizability, rendering it highly
susceptible to noise points. Additionally, instances occurred where models
built on larger datasets exhibit consistent or even inferior performance
compared to those on smaller datasets, a consequence of the interplay
between data redundancy61 and noise. When the data volume surpassed 30,
the ML model’s performance with random and interval sampling approa-
ched Latin hypercube sampling. This suggested that, with increasing data,
random and interval sampling progressively captured the majority of input-
output connections.
ML models built with datasets from RLHS exhibited poor general-
ization and highly unstable performance when the dataset count was below

Selection of surrogate model
A more accurate surrogate model can reduce the number of BO iterations
forachievingtheoptimalvalue62.Figure4 showstheR2andMAEresults of
the best UTS and EL prediction models on the initial squeeze process
dataset, along with a comparison of each model. Figures S4 and S5 of
Supplementary Information show detailed performance and hyper-
parameters of other models. For UTS prediction, it is notable that the
GPR, RF, XGBoost, and GBDT models suffered from severe overﬁtting
due to the limited dataset size. Although the Lasso model achieved the
highest R2 value (0.8142) and the lowest MAE value (4.1401) on the test
set, it still had notable errors in accurately predicting UTS. Consequently,
Lasso was selected as the UTS prediction surrogate model for sub-
sequent BO.
While the Lasso model exceled in predicting UTS, it fell short in pre-
dicting EL. Comparing models was essential to tackle overﬁtting in small
datasets. GBDT, Lasso, SVM, and BR models exhibited more pronounced
overﬁtting, suggesting that the ML model’s effectiveness was inﬂuenced not
only by the dataset size but also by the distribution of target values. XGBoost
model for EL prediction achieved the highest R2 value (0.7573) and the
lowest MAE value (0.4973) on the test set. Consequently, XGBoost was
chosen as the EL prediction surrogate model for subsequent BO.In contrast
to the UTS prediction surrogate model, the optimal EL surrogate model
(XGBoost) had a lower R2 and higher uncertainty. LASSO, a linear model,
suggests a multivariate linear relationship between process parameters and
UTS, while XGBoost, an ensemble method, captures the complex nonlinear
relationship between process parameters and EL. Figure 4c, f show the
distributionofUTSandELintrainingandtestsets.WhileUTSdistributions
are similar across the training and test sets, EL exhibits a different dis-
tribution. The discrepancy in dataset distribution negatively affects model
accuracy63, and together with the nonlinear relationship between process
parameters and EL, they lead to poor prediction performance for EL. This
makes it difﬁcult to accurately capture the EL distribution across the entire
process parameter set with the initial surrogate model.

(1 week), forming scheme design (2 weeks), mold development (8 weeks),

Discussion
To efﬁciently optimize casting processes with limitedsamples, we employed
an iterative design approach using BO. By leveraging the acquisition func-
tion of EI, whichincorporates predictedvalues and prediction uncertainties,
we systematically explored and exploited the design space to improve the
overall performance of castings.
In the BO process, model uncertainty is typically reduced through the
continuous addition of new observations14,62. The decrease in model
uncertainty signiﬁes a better understanding of the design space and reﬂects
the effectiveness of the optimization process. To showcase the reliability of
our strategy, Fig. 6a, b presented predicted values of iteratively updated ML
model using the selected process of each iteration as input and corre-
sponding R2. It is evident that the discrepancy between predicted and actual
properties decreases over the course of BO. As the iterative process
advances, the accumulation of data distribution insights gradually dimin-
ishes uncertainty.

model at this point, it tended to focus on the exploitation of familiar areas,
potentially resulting in diminishing returns with continued iteration.
Additionally, considering casting costs and indicator satisfaction, we
ceased optimization after the sixth iteration.
The properties of squeeze castings are inﬂuenced by the intricate
interplay of multiple process parameters. To comprehensively analyze
the impact of these parameters, we employed SHAP72 to provide
explanatory power to our model, as shown in Fig. 7. SHAP utilizes data
from the sixth iteration and the trained model. In Fig. 7a, c, the
rankings of process parameters’ importance for UTS and EL are
presented, respectively. Additionally, Fig. 7b, d illustrates the inﬂu-
ence of process parameters on the model’s output for both UTS and
EL. The horizontal axis represents the SHAP value, while the vertical
axis corresponds to distinct process parameters, with each point
denoting its respective value. The intensity of color conveys the
magnitude of the parameter: redder tones indicate higher values, while
bluer hues indicate lower values. A positive/negative SHAP value
indicates that the process value can increase/decrease the output of
the model.
The squeeze pressure emerges as the primary inﬂuencing factor for
UTS and EL of castings. Figure 7a demonstrates a positive correlation
between squeeze pressure and UTS, while Fig. 7c reveals that appropriate
squeeze pressure is crucial for achieving increased EL. Higher pressure
enhances undercooling, reduces the critical nucleation radius, and fosters
additional nucleation formation. Simultaneously, it eliminates the air gap
between the casting and mold, hastening cooling appropriately73. However,
excessive squeeze pressure introduces elevated residual stress and defor-
mation, resulting in reduced EL. Similarly, the dwell time exhibits a similar
impactpatternonEL,asevidencedbydecreasedELobservedintheiteration
1 with a dwell time of 30 s in Table 1.
Dwell time, die temperature, and pouring temperature have similar
importance for UTS, while the inﬂuence of squeeze velocity is minimal,
consistent with ﬁndings by Zhou et al.42. This can be attributed to discharge
effect of pressure in squeeze casting on the entrained air, highlighting the
synergistic effect between pressure and velocity.
Additionally, UTS and EL have distinct pouring temperature needs.
UTS beneﬁts from lower pouring temperatures, which accelerate solidiﬁ-
cation and reﬁne the grain structure. However, for EL, lower pouring
temperatures lead to premature solidiﬁcation, while excessive residual
pressure can reduce EL by causing deformation. Therefore, optimizing
squeeze casting involves carefully balancing pouring temperature and
squeeze pressure to achieve the best overall performance.
A thorough grasp of how casting technology inﬂuences microstructure
evolution during solidiﬁcation can enhance understanding of the prediction
anddesignofMLmodels.Phase-ﬁeldsimulationbyEasyPhasesoftwarewas
used to elucidate the optimization mechanism in our strategy.
Pressure and temperature signiﬁcantly impact casting mechanical
propertiesaccordingtoFig.7.Figure8illustratesthesolidiﬁcationprocessof
ZL101 alloy under different pouring temperatures and squeeze pressure
using PFM. The results indicate that at constant pressure, microstructural
changesbetweenadjacenttemperaturestepsareinsigniﬁcant,butnoticeable
differences occur over the full temperature range (690 °C to 740 °C). Higher
pouring temperature extends solidiﬁcation time and promotes dendrite
coarsening.
Furthermore, increased pressure boosts nucleation and accelerates
solidiﬁcation, reﬁning the microstructure more prominently than tem-
perature changes. With increasing pressure, adverse effects from high

pouring temperatures are mitigated according to simulation results of
solidiﬁcation of ZL101 alloy at varied pouring temperatures under a
130 MPa pressure in Fig. 8. Higher pressure results in a more reﬁned
microstructure, decreasing its sensitivity to temperature changes. Haider
and Mufti74 also emphasized the need to align suitable thermal para-
meters for high pressure in squeeze casting. At a pouring temperature of
720 °C, the microstructure simulation results at 130 MPa and 120 MPa
pressures are similar. The research showed that there is a peak in the
promoting effect of pressure73. Exceeding the optimal pressure ceases to
enhance the microstructure. Notably, in practical squeeze casting,
excessive pressure may adversely impact mechanical properties, as the
interplay of severe plastic deformation and high temperature can lead to
grain coarsening75. This explains why UTS did not improve, and EL
decreased during iteration 6 in Table 1, despite the pressure increasing to
140 MPa. The PFM simulation results in Fig. 8 also depict that as pressure
increased, the morphology of eutectic Si tends to be interrupted and its
distribution more dispersed.
Figure 9a, b depict the three-dimensional temperature distribution of
ZL101 alloy under varying pressures, while Fig. 9c shows the changes in
solid fraction corresponding to Fig. 8. In the initial solidiﬁcation phase, the
diffusion of latent heat from the center to the surroundings results in higher
temperatures in the dendritic arms near the center and lower temperatures
near the boundary. Owing to the low heat conduction rate and latent heat
release in the central region, a consistently high temperature is maintained.
As solidiﬁcation progresses, heightened pressure expedites thermal diffu-
sion, leading to a quicker temperature decrease at the boundary and the
centerof the dendrite tip. It is noteworthy that while the inﬂuence of a single
process parameter on properties can be explained, high-quality castings are
the outcome of multiple process parameters working in concert. Process
parameters can interact with each other and have nonlinear effects on the
casting properties.
